claim: Replication-dependent (RD) core histone mRNA produced during S-phase is the only known metazoan protein-coding mRNA presenting a 3' stem-loop instead of the otherwise universal polyA tail.
source: Replication-dependent (RD) core histone mRNA produced during S-phase is the only known metazoan protein-coding mRNA presenting a 3' stem-loop instead of the otherwise universal polyA tail.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about histone mRNA structure in metazoans.

claim: CPSF73 is a metallo β-lactamase (MBL) fold enzyme.
source: A metallo β-lactamase (MBL) fold enzyme, cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 73 (CPSF73), is proposed to be the sole endonuclease responsible for 3' end processing of both mRNA classes.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript and established knowledge about CPSF73 structure.

claim: CPSF73 is proposed to be the sole endonuclease responsible for 3' end processing of both RD histone pre-mRNA and normal protein-coding pre-mRNA.
source: A metallo β-lactamase (MBL) fold enzyme, cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 73 (CPSF73), is proposed to be the sole endonuclease responsible for 3' end processing of both mRNA classes.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing hypothesis in the field, supported by citations.

claim: MBLAC1 is an additional endoribonuclease selective for 3' processing of RD histone pre-mRNA during the S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: We report cellular, genetic, biochemical, substrate selectivity, and crystallographic studies providing evidence that an additional endoribonuclease, MBL domain containing protein 1 (MBLAC1), is selective for 3' processing of RD histone pre-mRNA during the S-phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Depletion of MBLAC1 in cells significantly affects cell cycle progression.
source: Depletion of MBLAC1 in cells significantly affects cell cycle progression thus identifying MBLAC1 as a new type of S-phase-specific cancer target.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and cell cycle analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBLAC1 is a new type of S-phase-specific cancer target.
source: Depletion of MBLAC1 in cells significantly affects cell cycle progression thus identifying MBLAC1 as a new type of S-phase-specific cancer target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell cycle effects observed upon MBLAC1 depletion.

claim: Production of core histone proteins (H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) is coordinated with DNA replication during S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: During S-phase of the cell cycle, production of the core histone proteins (H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) is coordinated with DNA replication (Harris et al., 1991; Ewen, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Metazoan mRNAs encoding for replication-dependent core histones lack the normal polyA tail.
source: Metazoan mRNAs encoding for the 'replication-dependent' (RD) core histones lack the normal polyA tail formed by 3' end hydrolysis of pre-mRNA followed by polyadenylation (Proudfoot, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: RD histone pre-mRNA undergoes endonucleolytic cleavage at the 3' side of an RNA hairpin producing mRNA with a 3' stem loop.
source: Instead, they undergo endonucleolytic cleavage at the 3ʹ side of an RNA hairpin (stem loop) producing mRNA with a 3´stem loop (SL), which is exported from the nucleus for use in translation (Marzluff et al., 2008; Marzluff and Koreski, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Replication-independent histone variant pre-mRNAs are normally polyadenylated and constitutively expressed during the cell cycle.
source: By contrast, the pre-mRNA of replication-independent histone variants are normally polyadenylated and constitutively expressed during the cell cycle (Marzluff et al., 2002; Wagner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CPSF73 is responsible for the hydrolysis of both RD histone pre-mRNA and normal protein-coding pre-mRNA.
source: A single endonuclease, cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 73 (CPSF73), is proposed to be responsible for the hydrolysis of both RD histone pre-mRNA (SL) and normal protein-coding pre-mRNA (polyA) (Dominski et al., 2005; Mandel et al., 2006; Kolev et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2009b; Dominski, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different macromolecular complexes are recruited to RD histone pre-mRNA versus normal protein-coding pre-mRNA despite both requiring hydrolytic reactions.
source: Although maturation of both classes of RNAs requires a hydrolytic reaction, different macromolecular complexes are recruited to the different pre-mRNA classes (SL or polyA) (Kolev et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SLBP, FLASH, and U7snRNP are specific factors involved in RD histone pre-mRNA maturation.
source: Specific factors involved in RD histone pre-mRNA maturation are the stem loop binding protein (SLBP), the FLICE-associated huge protein (FLASH), and the U7 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U7snRNP) that binds to a histone downstream element (HDE) (Dominski et al., 2005; Kolev et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Defective 3' end processing of RD histone pre-mRNA results in the generation of extended transcripts downstream of the HDE sequence.
source: Defective 3ʹ end processing of RD histone pre-mRNA, caused by depletion of factors including CPSF73, SLBP, Sm-like protein 11 (Lsm11), CstF64 or FLASH, results in the generation of extended transcripts downstream of the HDE sequence (Sullivan et al., 2009a; Romeo et al., 2014; Sullivan et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Misprocessed RD histone pre-mRNA can undergo polyadenylation using a secondary polyadenylation signal sequence downstream of the HDE in Drosophila melanogaster and humans.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster and humans, misprocessed RD histone pre-mRNA has been observed to undergo polyadenylation involving utilization of a secondary polyadenylation signal sequence located downstream of the HDE (Sullivan et al., 2009b; Romeo et al., 2014; Kari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of factors belonging to the 5' cap-binding complex (CBC) results in extended RD histone pre-mRNA transcripts.
source: Depletion of factors belonging to the 5ʹ cap-binding complex (CBC) (Hallais et al., 2013, Narita et al., 2007; Gruber et al., 2012), or to the cleavage factor II (CF IIm), which is normally involved in 3ʹ end processing of normal protein-coding pre-mRNA (polyA) (Hallais et al., 2013; de Vries et al., 2000), also results in extended RD histone pre-mRNA transcripts (Hallais et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of cleavage factor II (CF IIm) results in extended RD histone pre-mRNA transcripts.
source: Depletion of factors belonging to the 5ʹ cap-binding complex (CBC) (Hallais et al., 2013, Narita et al., 2007; Gruber et al., 2012), or to the cleavage factor II (CF IIm), which is normally involved in 3ʹ end processing of normal protein-coding pre-mRNA (polyA) (Hallais et al., 2013; de Vries et al., 2000), also results in extended RD histone pre-mRNA transcripts (Hallais et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a complex and dynamic relationship between factors involved in different stages of RD histone pre-mRNA transcription process.
source: These observations suggest a complex and dynamic relationship between the factors involved in the different stages of the RD histone pre-mRNA transcription process, which may involve participation of factors normally belonging to the polyA mRNA processing machinery.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations about factor depletion effects.

claim: Histone deacetylase and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors are cancer medicines that target proteins involved in the S-phase.
source: Important cancer medicines, including histone deacetylase and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, target proteins involved in the S-phase (Newbold et al., 2016; Falkenberg and Johnstone, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MBL-fold proteins are involved in nucleic acid hydrolysis.
source: In work aimed at identifying potential new S-phase cancer targets, we considered known and potential roles of MBL-fold proteins involved in nucleic acid hydrolysis (Dominski, 2007; Pettinati et al., 2016; Daiyasu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CPSF73 and CPSF100 are involved in pre-mRNA processing.
source: In addition, to the role of CPSF73, and the likely pseudo-enzyme CPSF100, in pre-mRNA processing (Dominski et al., 2005; Mandel et al., 2006), MBL-fold nucleases are involved in DNA repair (SNM1A-C nucleases) (Yan et al., 2010), snRNA processing (INTS9 and INTS11), and tRNA processing (ELAC 1 and 2) (Skaar et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SNM1A-C nucleases are MBL-fold nucleases involved in DNA repair.
source: In addition, to the role of CPSF73, and the likely pseudo-enzyme CPSF100, in pre-mRNA processing (Dominski et al., 2005; Mandel et al., 2006), MBL-fold nucleases are involved in DNA repair (SNM1A-C nucleases) (Yan et al., 2010), snRNA processing (INTS9 and INTS11), and tRNA processing (ELAC 1 and 2) (Skaar et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: INTS9 and INTS11 are MBL-fold nucleases involved in snRNA processing.
source: In addition, to the role of CPSF73, and the likely pseudo-enzyme CPSF100, in pre-mRNA processing (Dominski et al., 2005; Mandel et al., 2006), MBL-fold nucleases are involved in DNA repair (SNM1A-C nucleases) (Yan et al., 2010), snRNA processing (INTS9 and INTS11), and tRNA processing (ELAC 1 and 2) (Skaar et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ELAC1 and ELAC2 are MBL-fold nucleases involved in tRNA processing.
source: In addition, to the role of CPSF73, and the likely pseudo-enzyme CPSF100, in pre-mRNA processing (Dominski et al., 2005; Mandel et al., 2006), MBL-fold nucleases are involved in DNA repair (SNM1A-C nucleases) (Yan et al., 2010), snRNA processing (INTS9 and INTS11), and tRNA processing (ELAC 1 and 2) (Skaar et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The functions of MBLAC1 were unassigned prior to this study.
source: Whilst most of the ~18 human MBL-fold proteins have established functions (Pettinati et al., 2016), the functions of several are unassigned, including the MBL domain containing protein 1 (MBLAC1).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the study.

claim: MBLAC1 has an overall MBL fold.
source: Crystallographic and biochemical studies show that MBLAC1 has an overall MBL fold and di-zinc ion containing active site related to that of CPSF73, but which has distinctive structural features involving active site flanking loops and the absence of the β-CASP domain, which is only present in CPSF73.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBLAC1 has a di-zinc ion containing active site related to that of CPSF73.
source: Crystallographic and biochemical studies show that MBLAC1 has an overall MBL fold and di-zinc ion containing active site related to that of CPSF73, but which has distinctive structural features involving active site flanking loops and the absence of the β-CASP domain, which is only present in CPSF73.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic and ICP-MS data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBLAC1 has distinctive structural features involving active site flanking loops compared to CPSF73.
source: Crystallographic and biochemical studies show that MBLAC1 has an overall MBL fold and di-zinc ion containing active site related to that of CPSF73, but which has distinctive structural features involving active site flanking loops and the absence of the β-CASP domain, which is only present in CPSF73.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBLAC1 lacks the β-CASP domain that is present in CPSF73.
source: Crystallographic and biochemical studies show that MBLAC1 has an overall MBL fold and di-zinc ion containing active site related to that of CPSF73, but which has distinctive structural features involving active site flanking loops and the absence of the β-CASP domain, which is only present in CPSF73.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBLAC1 depletion from cells leads to the production of unprocessed RD histone pre-mRNA due to inefficient 3' end processing.
source: MBLAC1 depletion from cells leads to the production of unprocessed RD histone pre-mRNA due to inefficient 3ʹ end processing.
evidence: This is supported by ChrRNA-seq and RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Depletion of core histone proteins due to MBLAC1 depletion correlates with a cell cycle defect due to a delay in entering/progressing through S-phase.
source: The consequent depletion of core histone proteins correlates with a cell cycle defect due to a delay in entering/progressing through S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and western blot data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBLAC1 has been assigned as an RNAse Z and glyoxalase II subfamily enzyme based on sequence similarity studies.
source: On the basis of sequence similarity studies MBLAC1 has been assigned as an RNAse Z and glyoxalase II subfamily enzyme (Ridderström et al., 1996; Sievers et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statement about previous classification supported by citations.

claim: Recombinant MBLAC1 prepared from E. coli has only low, likely non-specific, glyoxalase activity.
source: However, we found that recombinant MBLAC1 prepared from E. coli has only low, likely non-specific, glyoxalase activity as observed for other hMBL-fold proteins belonging to the same subfamily (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the authors' biochemical assays.

claim: The MBLAC1 crystal structure was solved at 1.8 Å resolution in space group P1.
source: To investigate its function, we solved a crystal structure of MBLAC1 (1.8 Å resolution, space group P1) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: MBLAC1 structure reveals a stereotypical αββα MBL-fold.
source: The structure reveals a stereotypical αββα MBL- fold (Carfi et al., 1995) with two central mixed β-sheets (I and II), comprised of 8 and 5 strands respectively, surrounded by helices (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MBLAC1 has four of the five characteristic MBL-metal-binding motifs.
source: MBLAC1 has four of the five characteristic MBL-metal-binding motifs (Pettinati et al., 2016), His116, His118 Asp120 and His121 (motif II), His196 (motif III), Asp221 (motif IV) and His263 (motif V) (Figure 1B) (using BBL numbering) (Galleni et al., 2001) with two waters completing metal coordination.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the structure of recombinant MBLAC1 produced in E. coli, the active site was refined with two iron ions present.
source: In the structure of recombinant MBLAC1 produced in E. coli, the active site was refined with two iron ions present (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic refinement data.

claim: MBLAC1 produced in HEK293 cells preferentially binds zinc ions.
source: However, MBLAC1 produced in HEK293 cells preferentially binds zinc ions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ICP-MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Four MBLAC1 molecules are present in the crystallographic asymmetric unit.
source: Four MBLAC1 molecules (chains A-D) are present in the crystallographic asymmetric unit; analysis of interactions at the crystallographically observed monomer interfaces (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) identified interactions between chains A-B and C-D (Figure 1D) possibly reflecting dimeric MBLAC1 in solution (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and PISA analysis.

claim: MBLAC1 is possibly dimeric in solution.
source: Four MBLAC1 molecules (chains A-D) are present in the crystallographic asymmetric unit; analysis of interactions at the crystallographically observed monomer interfaces (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) identified interactions between chains A-B and C-D (Figure 1D) possibly reflecting dimeric MBLAC1 in solution (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by MALS and native PAGE data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The metal containing active site of MBLAC1 is adjacent to the dimer interface.
source: The metal containing active site is adjacent to the dimer interface (Figure 1D), rationalizing reduced dimerization as manifested by metal ligand substitution or metal removal (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and biophysical data shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: Metal ligand substitution or metal removal reduces MBLAC1 dimerization.
source: The metal containing active site is adjacent to the dimer interface (Figure 1D), rationalizing reduced dimerization as manifested by metal ligand substitution or metal removal (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by MALS and native PAGE data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Unsynchronised HeLa cells depleted for MBLAC1 show a cell cycle defect manifested by increased accumulation of cells in G1/early S-phase and decreased proportions of cells in G2.
source: Flow cytometry reveals that unsynchronised cells depleted for MBLAC1 show a cell cycle defect (Figure 2A). This is manifested by increased accumulation of cells in G1/early S-phase and decreased proportions of cells in G2 compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MBLAC1 depleted cells synchronised in early S-phase display a strong delay in G1/early S-phase 4 hours post-release.
source: Furthermore, cells synchronised in early S-phase using a double thymidine block (Harper, 2005) and harvested immediately after block release show the expected G1/early S phenotype (Figure 2A). However, 4 hours post-release, control cells progressed normally through the cell cycle, while MBLAC1 depleted cells displayed a strong delay in G1/early S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cyclin D1 is strongly upregulated with MBLAC1 depletion.
source: Western blots were then used to investigate the nature of the delay in cell cycle progression by monitoring levels of cyclin D1, a cell cycle protein marker expressed during G1 (Darzynkiewicz et al., 1996) (Figure 2B). Cyclin D1 was hardly detectable in controls, but was strongly upregulated with MBLAC1 depletion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MBLAC1 is present in both the cytosol and nucleus of wild-type HeLa cells.
source: Western blot analyses reveal the presence of MBLAC1 in both the cytosol and nucleus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A fraction of MBLAC1 localises in the nuclear compartment during early S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: However, a fraction of MBLAC1 was consistently observed to localise in the nuclear compartment during early S-phase of the cell cycle (and less consistently at later S-phase time points), suggesting a cell-cycle-dependent nuclear function for MBLAC1.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MBLAC1 has a cell-cycle-dependent nuclear function.
source: However, a fraction of MBLAC1 was consistently observed to localise in the nuclear compartment during early S-phase of the cell cycle (and less consistently at later S-phase time points), suggesting a cell-cycle-dependent nuclear function for MBLAC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of nuclear localization during early S-phase.

claim: Both MBLAC1 and CPSF73 depleted cells are impaired in efficiently entering/progressing in S-phase.
source: The abundance of BrdU positive cells, corresponding to S-phase cells, was strongly reduced in MBLAC1 and CPSF73 knockdowns at early time points (30 min, 1 hr), compared to controls (Figure 3A, left graph). Subsequent time points displayed a reduced difference, though 6 hr post release a consistent pool of G1 cells was still apparent in MBLAC1-depleted cells compared to both control and CPSF73-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). These results indicate that both MBLAC1 and, as expected, CPSF73 depleted cells are impaired in efficiently entering/progressing in S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The cell cycle defect is more pronounced with MBLAC1 depletion over the full cell cycle compared to CPSF73 depletion.
source: Although both depletions displayed a delay 30 min post-release, the defect was more pronounced with MBLAC1 depletion over the full cell cycle, implying a cell-cycle-specific role for MBLAC1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MBLAC1 levels increase 6 hr post-release from double thymidine block in control samples.
source: Western blot analyses indicated that in control samples (siLuc) MBLAC1 levels were increased 6 hr post-release (Figure 3B) corresponding to mid S-phase (as shown by flow cytometry profiles, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CPSF73 expression levels are relatively constant across the cell cycle.
source: By contrast, CPSF73 expression levels were relatively constant across the cell cycle (18 hr), consistent with its broad role in pre-mRNA processing (Mandel et al., 2006) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cyclin D1 levels are strongly upregulated with MBLAC1 depletion.
source: As described above, cyclin D1 levels were strongly upregulated with MBLAC1 depletion, while cyclin E levels were reduced compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cyclin E levels are reduced with MBLAC1 depletion compared to controls.
source: As described above, cyclin D1 levels were strongly upregulated with MBLAC1 depletion, while cyclin E levels were reduced compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CPSF73 depletion shows intermediate levels of cyclins D1 and E compared to MBLAC1 depletion and controls.
source: Notably for CPSF73 depletion, cyclins D1 and E showed intermediate levels compared to MBLAC1 depletion and controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Histone H3 levels are reduced in MBLAC1 depleted cells.
source: Given the strong correlation between S-phase and histone biosynthesis (Harris et al., 1991; Ewen, 2000), histone H3 levels were used to analyse RD histone protein abundance in MBLAC1 and CPSF73 depleted cells. Notably, H3 levels were reduced in MBLAC1 depleted cells; by contrast, CPSF73 depletion showed an intermediate H3 level compared to controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CPSF73 depletion shows an intermediate H3 level compared to controls.
source: Given the strong correlation between S-phase and histone biosynthesis (Harris et al., 1991; Ewen, 2000), histone H3 levels were used to analyse RD histone protein abundance in MBLAC1 and CPSF73 depleted cells. Notably, H3 levels were reduced in MBLAC1 depleted cells; by contrast, CPSF73 depletion showed an intermediate H3 level compared to controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MBLAC1 stable knockdown generated by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing shows a more severe phenotype than siRNA-mediated knockdown.
source: A more severe phenotype was observed in an MBLAC1 stable knockdown (Figure 3A right graph, C, D) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C) generated in HeLa cells by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and western blot data shown in Figure 3A, C, D.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 depletion of MBLAC1 results in altered production of cyclin E and reduced level of H3.
source: As for the siRNA-mediated knockdown experiments, CRISPR/Cas9 depletion of MBLAC1 results in an altered production of cyclin E and reduced level of H3.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cyclin D1 levels appear unchanged in MBLAC1 CRISPR/Cas9 knockdown, possibly due to cellular adaptation.
source: By contrast, cyclin D1 levels appear unchanged, possibly due to a mechanism of cellular adaptation under unfavourable conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GAPDH displays clear transcription termination defects downstream of the TES in CPSF73, but not MBLAC1, depleted cells.
source: Chromatin RNA-seq (ChrRNA-seq) analyses for a typical polyA mRNA encoding gene, for example glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), displayed clear transcription termination defects downstream of the transcription end site (TES) in CPSF73, but not MBLAC1, depleted cells, nor in a siRNA controls (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ChrRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RD histone genes show apparent transcription termination defects in both CPSF73 and MBLAC1 depletions.
source: Unexpectedly, RD histone genes (SL) showed apparent transcription termination defects, not only in CPSF73, but also in MBLAC1, depletions (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ChrRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 29 out of 43 non-overlapping RD histone genes manifested clear transcription termination defects in both MBLAC1 and CPSF73-depleted samples.
source: Importantly, 43 non-overlapping RD histone genes were analysed; of these 29 RD histone genes manifested clear transcription termination defects, in both the MBLAC1 and CPSF73-depleted samples (evidence for/exceptions are HIST1H2AI and HIST4H4 genes on which CPSF73 depletion apparently does not show an effect); a possible effect was observed on 7 RD histone genes (Figure 4—figure supplements 2,3), and no apparent effect was detected on seven remaining RD histone genes (Figure 4—figure supplements 2,4).
evidence: This is supported by ChrRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3, 4.

claim: Read through transcripts corresponding to transcription termination defects were detectable covering ~200 bases downstream of the TES with RD histone genes.
source: Where observed, read through (RT) transcripts corresponding to this defect were detectable covering ~200 bases downstream of the transcription end site (TES) with the RD histone genes (Figure 4—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: This is supported by ChrRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 3.

claim: MBLAC1 and CPSF73 may affect overlapping sets of histone genes, but to different extents.
source: The comparison of the read through of MBLAC1 to that of CPSF73 depletion shows a similar transcription termination defect pattern affecting similar genes with a few exceptions (Figure 4—figure supplements 2,4); it is possible that both MBLAC1 and CPSF73 may affect overlapping sets of histone genes, but to different extents.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ChrRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2, 4.

claim: RT-qPCR analyses validated the transcriptomics results showing GAPDH transcription termination is substantially affected by CPSF73, but not MBLAC1, depletion.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analyses validated the transcriptomics results. With normal protein-coding mRNA (GAPDH), transcription termination was substantially affected by CPSF73, but not MBLAC1, depletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The abundance of termination defective RD histone mRNA increased in both MBLAC1- and CPSF73-depleted cells compared to controls.
source: The abundance of termination defective (3ʹ end extended) RD histone mRNA increased in both MBLAC1- and CPSF73-depleted cells compared to controls (Figure 4D) supporting the proposal that MBLAC1 is a RD histone selective pre-mRNA processing enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MBLAC1 is a RD histone selective pre-mRNA processing enzyme.
source: The abundance of termination defective (3ʹ end extended) RD histone mRNA increased in both MBLAC1- and CPSF73-depleted cells compared to controls (Figure 4D) supporting the proposal that MBLAC1 is a RD histone selective pre-mRNA processing enzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR data.

claim: MBLAC1 CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown cells show increased abundance of termination defective RD histone mRNA compared to wildtype HeLa cells.
source: Single gene analyses on chrRNA confirmed the increased abundance of termination defective (3ʹ end extended) RD histone mRNA in MBLAC1 CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown cells compared to wildtype HeLa cells, after synchronization in early S-phase (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There is a low (~15%) but consistent increase in polyA+ histone transcripts in MBLAC1-depleted cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analyses showed a low (~15%), but consistent, increase in polyA +histone transcripts in MBLAC1-depleted cells compared to wild-type cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RD histone pre-mRNA can undergo polyadenylation when inefficiently processed at their normal 3' processing site.
source: These observations support previous studies (Sullivan et al., 2009b; Romeo et al., 2014; Kari et al., 2013), by implying that RD histone pre-mRNA can undergo polyadenylation when inefficiently processed at their normal 3' processing site.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the polyA selection data and supported by citations.

claim: MBLAC1 specifically associates with chromatin associated histone mRNA during early S-phase.
source: The results provided evidence that MBLAC1 specifically associates with chromatin associated histone mRNA during early S-phase, but that it either does not interact, or interacts to a lesser extent (similarly to FLASH) (Figure 4F–G), with normal protein coding mRNA (GAPDH); a similar amount of FLASH was recruited on histone RNA compared to MBLAC1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-ChIP data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: MBLAC1 either does not interact, or interacts to a lesser extent with normal protein coding mRNA (GAPDH).
source: The results provided evidence that MBLAC1 specifically associates with chromatin associated histone mRNA during early S-phase, but that it either does not interact, or interacts to a lesser extent (similarly to FLASH) (Figure 4F–G), with normal protein coding mRNA (GAPDH); a similar amount of FLASH was recruited on histone RNA compared to MBLAC1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-ChIP data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: RD histone mRNA relative levels are not affected by the tagging of MBLAC1.
source: Note that RD histone mRNA relative levels are not affected by the tagging of MBLAC1 as observed by comparison of wild-type and MBLAC1 C-terminal FLAG knock HeLa cells RNA-ChIP input samples (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-ChIP input data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Recombinant wild-type MBLAC1 purified from E. coli displays significant nonspecific ribonucleolytic activity.
source: Recombinant wtMBLAC1 purified from E. coli bacteria displayed significant nonspecific ribonucleolytic activity, degrading the substrate in a time dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The H196A/D221A/H263A variant of MBLAC1 manifests very little ribonucleolytic activity.
source: By contrast, mutMBLAC1 manifested very little activity over time under the same assay conditions.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Wild-type MBLAC1 purified from HEK293 cells gives an apparently more specific cleavage pattern than E. coli produced MBLAC1.
source: Notably, the endoribonucleolytic activity of wtMBLAC1 purified from HEK293 cells using the same α 32P UTP-labeled histone RNA fragment gave an apparently more specific cleavage pattern. In particular, cleavage products corresponding in size to the biologically authentic 5' and 3' fragments were manifested (Figure 5C) (shown by red arrows).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The more specific cleavage by HEK293 produced MBLAC1 may reflect different kinetic properties, possibly resulting from post-translational modifications, or more biologically correct metal complexation at the active site.
source: This apparently more specific cleavage by wtMBLAC1 when produced in HEK293 cells may reflect different kinetic properties, possibly resulting from post-translational modifications, or more biologically correct metal complexation at the active site (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for the observed differences.

claim: Bacterially produced wild-type MBLAC1 shows clear ribonucleolytic activity with wild-type RNA substrate in a time-dependent manner.
source: Bacterially produced wtMBLAC1 showed clear ribonucleolytic activity with the WT RNA substrate in a time-dependent manner (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Major cleavage products by MBLAC1 are observed at positions corresponding to the authentic 3' processing position.
source: Major cleavage products were observed (red arrow) at positions corresponding to the authentic 3' processing position.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Little evidence for ribonucleolytic activity was observed when wild-type MBLAC1 was incubated with MUT RNA (A/G substitution at cleavage site).
source: However, little evidence for ribonucleolytic activity was observed when wtMBLAC1 was incubated with MUT RNA (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MBLAC1 specifically recognises the biologically authentic CA dinucleotide required for histone pre-mRNA maturation.
source: This observation suggests that MBLAC1 specifically recognises the biologically authentic CA dinucleotide required for histone pre-mRNA maturation and that this site is critical for recognition/initial cleavage/binding by MBLAC1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cleavage assay data with mutant RNA.

claim: Mononucleotides were not observed to accumulate under any of the tested conditions, implying a lack of exonucleolytic activity for MBLAC1.
source: Mononucleotides were not observed to accumulate under any of the tested conditions (data not shown) implying a lack of exonucleolytic activity for MBLAC1.
evidence: This is an observation from the cleavage assays.

claim: MBLAC1 is a ribonuclease with endonucleolytic activity.
source: Thus, consistent with the crystallographically observed structural similarity between MBLAC1 and LACTB2 (Levy et al., 2016) (Figure 1H), these results identify MBLAC1 as a ribonuclease with endonucleolytic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cleavage assay data and structural similarity.

claim: Isolated MBLAC1 appears more sequence selective than purified CPSF73, especially with shorter RNA substrates.
source: Unlike purified CPSF73 (Mandel et al., 2006), which exhibits substantially sequence-independent ribonuclease activity, isolated MBLAC1 appears more sequence selective especially with shorter RNA substrates (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a comparison of MBLAC1 activity with reported CPSF73 activity.

claim: Isolated MBLAC1 initially catalyses hydrolysis at the biologically validated CA cleavage site with subsequent endonucleolytic cleavage occurring at other positions.
source: These observations imply that, at least in isolated form, MBLAC1 initially catalyses hydrolysis at the biologically validated CA cleavage site with subsequent endonucleolytic cleavage occurring at other positions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cleavage assay data.

claim: SLBP appears to be necessary for efficient processing of histone pre-mRNA through stabilization of the HDE-U7 snRNA interaction.
source: Specific elements are required for maturation of histone pre-mRNA in vivo (Marzluff and Koreski, 2017); in particular, SLBP appears to be necessary for efficient processing through stabilization of the HDE-U7 snRNA interaction and the HLF complex involving symplekin, CPSF73, CPSF100, and CstF64, which are required for the cleavage of the pre-mRNA (Dominski et al., 1999; Kolev et al., 2008; Romeo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The HLF complex involving symplekin, CPSF73, CPSF100, and CstF64 is required for the cleavage of histone pre-mRNA.
source: Specific elements are required for maturation of histone pre-mRNA in vivo (Marzluff and Koreski, 2017); in particular, SLBP appears to be necessary for efficient processing through stabilization of the HDE-U7 snRNA interaction and the HLF complex involving symplekin, CPSF73, CPSF100, and CstF64, which are required for the cleavage of the pre-mRNA (Dominski et al., 1999; Kolev et al., 2008; Romeo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The reaction catalysed by MBLAC1 on wild-type RNA 1 generates two main products assigned as 27 and 29 nucleotides long, corresponding to the physiological major and minor cleavage sites.
source: The reaction catalysed by MBLAC1 on the wild-type RNA 1 generated two main products assigned as 27 and 29 nucleotides long (based on our fragment numbering system), corresponding to the 'physiological' major and minor cleavage sites (Streit et al., 1993; Furger et al., 1998), respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When a single nucleotide in RNA 1 is mutated at position 27 (A/G), a single main processing product corresponding to cleavage at position 29 is observed.
source: When a single nucleotide in RNA 1 is mutated at position 27 (A/G), to abolish the 'physiological' CA dinucleotide at this position (RNA 2), we observed production of a single main processing product corresponding to cleavage at position 29 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hydrolysis of RNA 2 (with A/G mutation at position 27) appears less efficient compared to that of RNA 1.
source: Although hydrolysis of RNA 2 was clearly observed, it appeared less efficient compared to that of RNA 1.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When the wild-type RNA is modified to contain only one CA dinucleotide at position 27 (RNA 3), incubation with MBLAC1 leads to production of a single observed degradation product consistent with cleavage at position 27.
source: To further investigate the specificity of cleavage after the CA at position 27, the wild-type RNA was modified to contain only one CA dinucleotide at position 27 (RNA 3). Incubation with MBLAC1 led to the production of a single observed degradation product consistent with cleavage at position 27 (major cleavage site), but again with apparently impaired efficiency (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When the nucleotide sequence of the stem-loop is inverted (RNA 4), the cleavage reaction appears less efficient, although the cleavage specificity is apparently not compromised.
source: When the nucleotide sequence of the stem-loop was inverted, to maintain secondary structure (RNA 4), the cleavage reaction appeared less efficient, although the cleavage specificity was apparently not compromised within our limits of detection (note that the processing products of RNA 4 has a slower electrophoretic mobility) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The precise stem-loop sequence composition does not affect the correct positioning of MBLAC1 at the physiological CA cleavage site.
source: This observation suggests the precise stem-loop sequence composition does not affect the correct positioning of MBLAC1 at the physiological CA cleavage site.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cleavage assay data with inverted stem-loop RNA.

claim: When the stem-loop sequence is modified to ablate its conformation (RNA 5), cleavage at position 27 is apparently completely abolished.
source: When the stem-loop sequence was modified to ablate its conformation (RNA 5), cleavage at position 27 (the major cleavage site) was apparently completely abolished; instead, a major band was observed corresponding to cleavage at the CA, position 23, although longer degradation fragments were also detected (consistent with cleavage at positions 29, and possibly 32, 35) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The stem-loop structure prevents MBLAC1 from accessing putative single-stranded cleavage sites located upstream of position 27, thus helping to maintain specificity of cleavage at position 27.
source: The degradation patterns observed for RNA 4 and 5 imply that likely the stem-loop structure prevents MBLAC1 from accessing putative single-stranded cleavage sites located upstream of position 27, thus helping to maintain specificity of cleavage at position 27.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cleavage assay data with modified stem-loop RNAs.

claim: MBLAC1 activity on a fragment lacking the HDE sequence (RNA 6) shows efficient cleavage is maintained and the major cleavage site (position 27) is still recognised, although the cleavage specificity is reduced.
source: MBLAC1 activity was also evaluated on a fragment lacking the HDE sequence (RNA 6); interestingly, with this substrate efficient cleavage was maintained and the major cleavage site (position 27) still recognised, although the cleavage specificity was reduced, leading to the formation of additional degradation bands corresponding to hydrolysis at all the CA dinucleotides present in the fragment 6 sequence (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Purified MBLAC1 displays significant histone mRNA 3' end processing specificity.
source: Overall, these results support the proposal that purified MBLAC1 displays significant histone mRNA 3' end processing specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro cleavage assay data with various RNA substrates.

claim: MBLAC1 is an endoribonuclease selective for 3' end processing of RD histone pre-mRNA during S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: The combined biochemical, cellular, and genetic analyses presented here provide clear evidence that MBLAC1 is an endoribonuclease selective for 3' end processing of RD histone pre-mRNA during S-phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Isolated recombinant MBLAC1 is selective for hydrolytic cleavage at the biologically relevant CA dinucleotides present 5 and 7 nucleotides downstream of the stem-loop sequence in replication-dependent pre-mRNA.
source: Assays with isolated recombinant MBLAC1 reveal it is selective for hydrolytic cleavage at the biologically relevant CA dinucleotides present 5 and 7 nucleotides downstream of the stem-loop sequence in replication-dependent pre-mRNA (positions 27 and 29, respectively, using our pre-mRNA numbering).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data.

claim: MBLAC1 is related to CPSF73 in terms of the overall fold of its MBL domain, but has distinctive structural features.
source: Crystallographic and other biophysical analyses support the assignment of MBLAC1 as a nuclease, which is related to CPSF73 in terms of the overall fold of its MBL domain, but which has distinctive, structural features, possibly reflecting their different substrate recognition and/or substrate binding modes (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and structural comparisons.

claim: The slow growth rate of MBLAC1-depleted cells likely reflects its important role in RD histone pre-mRNA processing which is required for normal progression through the cell cycle.
source: The slow growth rate of MBLAC1-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) likely reflects its important role in RD histone pre-mRNA processing which is required for normal progression through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the proliferation assay data.

claim: The observation of a cell cycle defect in entering/progressing through S-phase correlates with reduced histone protein abundance in HeLa cells after depletion of MBLAC1.
source: The observation of a cell cycle defect in entering/progressing through S-phase correlates with reduced histone protein abundance in HeLa cells after depletion of MBLAC1, either using siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The inability of MBLAC1-depleted cells to produce the appropriate amount of histone proteins due to the lack of mature mRNA encoding for them is consistent with occurrence of a 'G1-like' block.
source: The inability of MBLAC1-depleted cells to produce the appropriate amount of histone proteins due to the lack of mature mRNA encoding for them is also consistent with occurrence of a 'G1-like' block, as observed by flow-cytometry and western blot analyses (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell cycle and protein level data.

claim: During S-phase, MBLAC1 has a specialised role in RD histone pre-mRNA processing.
source: These results imply that during S-phase, MBLAC1 has a specialised role in RD histone pre-mRNA processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cellular and genetic data.

claim: The stem-loop secondary structure of RD nascent pre-mRNA is involved in enabling preferential cleavage at position 27.
source: Studies with recombinant MBLAC1 purified from human or E. coli cells, define MBLAC1 as an endoribonuclease, with selectivity for cleavage at the biologically authentic CA dinucleotides (positions 27 and 29 using our nomenclature, Figure 6). These results imply that the stem-loop secondary structure of RD nascent pre-mRNA is involved in enabling preferential cleavage at position 27.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro cleavage assay data.

claim: The presence of the HDE sequence appears to be required to avoid non-specific cleavage.
source: The presence of the HDE sequence appears to be required to avoid non-specific cleavage, although cleavage at position 27 was still observed when the HDE was removed (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The HDE is a major factor in defining the cleavage site of RD histone pre-mRNA.
source: The involvement of the HDE element in determining selectivity is supported by in vitro studies utilizing HeLa nuclear extracts indicating that the HDE is a major factor in defining the cleavage site of RD histone pre-mRNA (Scharl and Steitz, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Isolated MBLAC1 has potential to catalyse cleavage at CA sites other than at positions 27 and 29.
source: The work with isolated MBLAC1 reveals that it has potential to catalyse cleavage at CA sites other than at positions 27 and 29, although the biological relevance of these other reactions needs to be validated.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vitro cleavage assay data.

claim: It is possible that the observed in vitro sequence specificity of MBLAC1 may enable recognition of core histone pre-mRNA substrates without the requirement for as many additional factors as is necessary in the case of CPSF73.
source: Further detailed work is required to compressively define the factors responsible for targeting MBLAC1 to the RD histone pre-mRNA cleavage site. The available results indicate that it is possible that the observed in vitro sequence specificity of MBLAC1 may enable recognition of core histone pre-mRNA substrates without the requirement for as many additional factors as is necessary in the case of CPSF73 (or that MBLAC1 requires different factors) (Sullivan et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of MBLAC1 substrate recognition.

claim: CPSF73 promotes RD histone pre-mRNA processing.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Dominski et al., 2005; Kolev et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2009a), we found that CPSF73 promotes RD histone pre-mRNA processing.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data and citations to previous studies.

claim: CPSF73 is likely relatively more important than MBLAC1 in RD histone pre-mRNA processing outside of S-phase.
source: However, it is likely that CPSF73 is relatively more important than MBLAC1 in RD histone pre-mRNA processing outside of S-phase, reflecting its essential role in the biosynthesis of polyadenylated mRNA, including that of multiple histone variants (Marzluff et al., 2008; Marzluff et al., 2002; Wagner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the known roles of CPSF73 and the observed cell cycle-specific effects of MBLAC1.

claim: CPSF73 could be wholly or partly responsible for processing of defective RD histone pre-mRNA that subsequently undergoes polyadenylation when MBLAC1 is depleted in cells.
source: CPSF73 could well also be wholly or partly responsible for processing of defective RD histone pre-mRNA that subsequently undergoes polyadenylation (Sullivan et al., 2009b) when MBLAC1 is depleted in cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of CPSF73 in compensating for MBLAC1 depletion.

claim: It is possible that both CPSF73 and MBLAC1 selectively impact on the rates of maturation of different histone pre-mRNA substrates in vivo.
source: Reported biochemical work with CPSF73 in its isolated form has only been carried-out with few histone pre-mRNA model sequences (Kolev and Steitz, 2005). Thus, it is possible that both CPSF73 and MBLAC1 selectively impact on the rates of maturation of different histone pre-mRNA substrates in vivo, opening up the possibility for selective modulation of the biosynthesis of RD histone variants.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential differential effects of CPSF73 and MBLAC1 on different histone genes.

claim: MBLAC1 inhibition may selectively slow down S-phase progression in cancer cells.
source: Our genetic and cellular studies imply that MBLAC1 inhibition may selectively slow down S-phase progression in cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell cycle effects observed upon MBLAC1 depletion.

claim: MBLAC1 may represent a new S-phase specific cancer target.
source: Thus, MBLAC1 may represent a new S-phase specific cancer target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell cycle effects and the S-phase specificity of MBLAC1.

claim: Human MBL-fold endonucleases are likely amenable to small molecule targeting.
source: The true bacterial MBLs involved in antibacterial resistance have been shown to be amenable to small molecule targeting (Pettinati et al., 2016), and it is likely that human MBL-fold endonucleases will also be sensitive to small molecule inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the known druggability of bacterial MBLs.

claim: Targeting MBLAC1 may not be as toxic as targeting CPSF73.
source: Our results suggest that targeting MBLAC1 may not be as toxic as CPSF73, which has a pleiotropic role in polyadenylated pre-mRNA processing (Mandel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential therapeutic advantage of targeting MBLAC1.

claim: The development of MBLAC1 inhibitors, likely for use in combination with other drugs, is of interest from the cancer treatment perspective.
source: Thus, the development of MBLAC1 inhibitors, likely for use in combination with other drugs, is of interest from the cancer treatment perspective.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential therapeutic application of MBLAC1 inhibitors.

claim: Relatively non-selective zinc ion chelating compounds, including HDAC inhibitors such as SAHA, are already used for cancer treatment via S-phase targeting.
source: Finally, it is notable that relatively non-selective zinc ion chelating compounds, including HDAC inhibitors such as SAHA (suberanilohydroxamic acid) (West and Johnstone, 2014), are already used for cancer treatment via S-phase targeting.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: It is possible that zinc ion chelating compounds work, at least in part, by inhibiting metal dependent endoribonucleases, such as CPSF73 and MBLAC1.
source: It is possible that these, at least in part, work by inhibiting metal dependent endoribonucleases, such as CPSF73 and MBLAC1.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of action of existing cancer drugs.
